salsa.quote: The music style was based on the late [[son montuno]] of [[Arsenio Rodríguez]], [[Conjunto Chappottín]] and [[Roberto Faz]].
During the 1950s, New York became a hotspot of Mambo with musicians like the aforementioned Pérez Prado, [[Chano Pozo|Luciano "Chano" Pozo]], Mongo Santamaría, Machito and Tito Puente.
In 1966, the Palladium closed because it lost its liquor license.
During the late 1960s, the Dominican musician Johnny Pacheco and Italian-American businessman [[Jerry Masucci]] founded the recording company [[Fania Records]]
including Willie Colón, Celia Cruz, [[Larry Harlow (musician)|Larry Harlow]], [[Ray Barretto]], Héctor Lavoe and [[Ismael Miranda]]

Pacheco put together a team that included percussionist [[Louie Ramirez|Louie Ramírez]], bassist [[Bobby Valentín]] and arranger [[Larry Harlow (salsa)|Larry Harlow]] to form the [[Fania All-Stars]] in 1968
New York saw in the 1970s the first use of the term salsa to commercialize several styles of Latin dance music
presenting an all-embracing Puerto Rican, Pan-American or Latino sound with which the people from all of Latin America
In 1971, the Fania All-Stars sold out [[Yankee Stadium (1923)|Yankee Stadium]].
several Latin American countries, such as Colombia, Venezuela, Peru, Mexico and Panama, began producing their own salsa music
Two of the biggest stars from this period are [[Oscar D'León]] from Venezuela and [[Joe Arroyo]] from Colombia.
Some people say that D'León's performance gave momentum to a "salsa craze" that brought back some of the older templates and motivated the development of [[timba]].
